Fireworks, Nebius, and Hyperbolic all give you a small credit balance to test bigger models before committing to anything.

Perfect for AI agents, side projects, or just testing things out without spending a dollar.

f7n0PnnQq3Y.description:
Your agent ran all night and wrote 30,000 lines of code. Every check passed. The app was broken. The loop didn't fail — your system did, because nothing in it could stop and ask if you were still solving the right problem. You already did the smart thing and split one agent into a team: a planner, a builder, a reviewer. That's the graph. But connecting agents isn't the same as putting someone in charge. The fix isn't a smarter model — it's a governance layer, an operating system for your agents. And the part you can build today is simple: every decision in your system has exactly one owner.

→ Countable things belong to CODE — budget limits, retry counts, valid JSON, tests passing; never ask a model to check what an IF statement can
→ Ambiguous things belong to the MODEL — why did this fail, the plan or the reviewer; let it diagnose, never let it decide alone
→ The mission belongs to YOU — not an approve button, the one person who owns what "done" actually means
→ That overnight disaster didn't need more intelligence; it needed code to stop the bleeding, a model to say why, and a human holding the goal
→ You already built half an operating system by accident — checkpoints, retries, permissions; the other half you build on purpose
→ A graph connects your agents. An operating system runs them.

fagSVgEtU2E.description:
The Demon Core was a 6.2 kilogram sphere of plutonium-gallium alloy, manufactured by the Manhattan Project in 1945 and originally intended for the third atomic bomb to be used against Japan. Japan surrendered before it was shipped, and the core remained at Los Alamos for testing.
On August 21, 1945, physicist Harry Daghlian was alone at the Omega Site, stacking tungsten carbide bricks around the core to study how close it could get to criticality. As he placed the final brick, neutron detectors indicated the assembly was going supercritical. He pulled his hand back, the brick slipped from his grip, and fell directly into the assembly. A flash of blue light filled the room. Daghlian dismantled the assembly by hand to stop the reaction, receiving an estimated whole-body dose of 290 to 310 rem, roughly 3 sieverts. He died 25 days later from acute radiation syndrome, the first person in history killed by a criticality accident.
Experiments with the core continued. On May 21, 1946, exactly nine months later, physicist Louis Slotin was performing a similar demonstration, holding a beryllium reflector dome apart from the core using the blade of a screwdriver rather than the required safety shims, a practice Enrico Fermi had specifically warned him would get him killed within a year. The screwdriver slipped. The dome closed. The room lit up blue again. Slotin, standing closest to the assembly, received an estimated dose of around 880 rem, roughly 8.8 sieverts, one of the most severe acute radiation exposures ever recorded in a survivable timeframe. He died 9 days later.
Remarkably, both accidents occurred on a Tuesday, both on the 21st of the month, and both men died in the same hospital room at the Los Alamos base hospital.
After Slotin's death, the core was permanently retired. It was melted down in the summer of 1946 and its plutonium recycled into other weapon cores. It was never assembled again.
Source: Atomic Heritage Foundation, Nuclear Museum. American Physical Society, This Month in Physics History (2014). Wikipedia, Harry Daghlian. Nevada Technical Associates, The Demon Core.

bG9KEqVKDtg.description:
Wormholes are considered among the most exotic theoretical objects in physics. They are hypothetical shortcuts through spacetime, connecting two distant locations through a tunnel structure known as the wormhole's throat, with an entrance and an exit.
The concept was first identified by Austrian physicist Ludwig Flamm in 1916, while he was reviewing Karl Schwarzschild's solution to Einstein's field equations. Flamm realised the mathematics allowed for a second solution, an invisible connection between two separate regions of spacetime. In 1935, Albert Einstein and physicist Nathan Rosen independently developed the concept further, publishing what is now known as the Einstein-Rosen bridge.
The idea comes directly from General Relativity. According to the theory, spacetime can be curved, and a wormhole is a region where that curvature becomes extreme enough to form a tunnel-like structure, theoretically connecting two distant points within the same universe, or even two separate universes. To date, no traversable wormhole has ever been observed.
There is also a structural problem. In 1962, John Wheeler and Robert Fuller showed that the Einstein-Rosen bridge is unstable. It collapses before even a photon can cross it. In 1988, Kip Thorne and Michael Morris showed that keeping a wormhole open long enough to traverse would require exotic matter, matter with negative energy density, something that has never been found in usable quantity anywhere in the universe.
And even in the hypothetical scenario where such matter existed and the wormhole stayed open, travelling through it would not be survivable. The gravitational difference between the entrance and the exit would generate tidal forces strong enough to pull the head and feet of anything passing through in opposite directions, the same mechanism that spaghettifies matter falling into a black hole. A 2026 study calculated that this stretching forms a complete barrier near the equator of the throat, destroying anything that passes too close to it.
So based on everything current physics understands, even if a wormhole existed today, we would still have no way to travel through it.
Source: Flamm, L. (1916). Physikalische Zeitschrift. Einstein, A. and Rosen, N. (1935). Physical Review. Wheeler, J.A. and Fuller, R.W. (1962). Physical Review. Morris, M.S. and Thorne, K.S. (1988). American Journal of Physics.

Anthropic just released their guide for rewriting an entire codebase with AI, and one of their own teams already used it to rewrite roughly a million lines of code from one language to another in under two weeks — with every test passing before merge. For twenty years a full rewrite was a multi-year, multi-million-dollar bet you deferred forever. That math just changed.

The real trick isn't that the AI writes code. It's a different way of working: you don't fix the code, you fix the process that produces it. When the same mistake shows up across many files, you don't hand-patch each one — you amend the one rule that caused it and regenerate the batch.

The three moves that make it work:
1. Build the JUDGE first — turn your existing tests into a parity harness that must pass on BOTH the old code and the new code. That's your exit condition.
2. Write a RULEBOOK, not code — one document answering every translation decision (types, errors, naming) before you touch a file.
3. Make the QUEUE mechanical — a file is done when its output exists on disk, so the migration is resumable by construction. Fan out translators in parallel with adversarial review.

Old cost of a million-line migration: ~$4M over 4 years. New token bill: ~$165K. Worst case now — delete the branch and try again tomorrow.

cR7pTKa2TyA.description:
Why do people hype quantum computing so much? Here is the actual reason.
A classical computer solves problems by exploring possibilities sequentially, one by one, checking each option until it finds the best answer. For small problems this is fast enough. But as the number of possibilities grows, the time needed to solve the problem grows exponentially. Problems that seem manageable at small scale become practically unsolvable at large scale.
A quantum computer works on a fundamentally different principle.
Instead of storing information in bits that are either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits called qubits. A qubit can exist in a superposition of both 0 and 1 simultaneously. This is not a metaphor. It is a direct consequence of quantum mechanics, the same physics that governs electrons, photons, and the fundamental behaviour of matter.
When a quantum algorithm runs, it does not check possibilities one by one. Instead it manipulates these superposed states using a phenomenon called quantum interference. Interference amplifies the probability of correct answers and cancels out the probability of incorrect ones simultaneously. IBM describes interference as the engine of quantum computing. The result is that for certain categories of problems, a quantum computer can explore an exponentially larger solution space far more efficiently than any classical machine.
This is why the applications are so significant. Designing new drug molecules requires simulating quantum interactions between atoms, which classical computers cannot do accurately at scale. Discovering new materials for batteries, semiconductors, or superconductors involves the same problem. Optimising global logistics across millions of variables simultaneously. These are exactly the kinds of problems where quantum interference gives quantum computers a structural advantage over classical systems.
In December 2024, Google's Willow quantum chip performed a specific calculation in five minutes that would take the world's fastest classical supercomputers approximately ten septillion years. That gap is not incremental. It is architectural.
The problems that would take classical computers centuries may take quantum computers hours. Not because quantum computers are faster versions of classical computers. But because they compute in a fundamentally different way.
Source: IBM, What Is Quantum Computing. Google, Willow Quantum Chip (2024). SpinQ, Quantum Interference in Quantum Computing (2025). Frontiers in Quantum Science and Technology, Quantum Computing Foundations (2025). Quantum Zeitgeist, Complete Guide to Quantum Computing (2026).

Q8oTuqZHt3c.description:
Your agent loop is one worker. You've been running it like it's the whole team.

The field just shifted from loop engineering to graph engineering — your loop becomes one node inside an organization of agents that share a goal. And here's the part nobody explains: you're not running one graph, you're running two at the same time. An org graph is your permanent roster — long-lived agents with named roles that always exist. A work graph is what's happening right now — tasks that spawn, split, merge, and disappear based on what the agents discover. The hard part: when one node fails in a graph, three agents downstream are working off stale inputs and none of them know it.

→ A loop is one agent's contract with itself: trigger, act, verify, retry — all in one context
→ A graph is an organization of agents where each node runs its own loop and edges define how work flows
→ The org graph is your permanent team roster — long-lived agents with named roles that always exist
→ The work graph rewrites itself mid-sprint — tasks spawn, split, merge, and disappear as evidence changes
→ When a node fails in a graph, the entire downstream goes stale — failure surface is way larger than a loop
→ A loop is one worker doing its job. A graph is the whole team, organized.

Comment "GRAPH" and I'll send you the breakdown with both graph types mapped out.

PbMpQ98witE.description:
The platypus lays eggs despite being a mammal. It sweats milk through its skin because it has no nipples. Its genome contains genes from reptiles, mammals, and birds simultaneously. And it glows green under ultraviolet light.
But even most people who know these facts do not know the stranger ones.
Male platypus have venomous spurs on their hind legs. The venom is not lethal but it produces hyperalgesia, an extreme sensitivity to pain, that can last for months after a single sting. It does not respond to conventional painkillers including morphine. There is no antivenom. There is no treatment. You simply wait it out.
Its bill contains two types of sensory receptors working simultaneously. Mechanoreceptors that detect pressure changes in the water, and electroreceptors that detect the electrical signals produced by the muscle contractions of nearby animals. This is the same electroreception system used by sharks, called passive electroreception. The platypus closes its eyes, ears, and nose completely when diving and hunts entirely through these signals. It can locate prey in total darkness through mud and silt with no visual information at all.
When scientists sequenced the platypus genome in 2008, they found something that genuinely confused them. The genome contained genes associated with reptiles, genes associated with birds, and genes associated with mammals, all present simultaneously in a single organism. The lead researcher described it as looking like it had been assembled from parts of different animals. It was the first mammal genome to reveal such a mosaic of evolutionary history.
In 2020, researchers from Northland College discovered that platypus fur is biofluorescent. Under ultraviolet light, the fur absorbs UV and emits visible light, glowing a bright blue-green colour. Scientists believe this may have evolved as a form of communication or camouflage in low light conditions.
Evolution did not design the platypus. It just kept adding things and never took anything away.
Source: Warren, W.C. et al. (2008). Genome analysis of the platypus reveals unique signatures of evolution. Nature. Anich, P.S. et al. (2020). Biofluorescence in the platypus. Mammalia. NHS, Platypus Venom Effects. National Geographic, Platypus Facts.

Uber just shipped an AI agent that builds your whole grocery cart from a photo of a handwritten list — and the interesting part for builders is how little the LLM actually does.

Their real architecture is a multi-prompt state graph, and most of the boxes are plain deterministic code. The LLM only handles the fuzzy stuff: reading what you meant, judging which product fits. Everything that has to be correct — prices, arithmetic, availability, the cart total — is code the model never touches.

→ The planner LLM doesn't "go shopping" — it emits a structured CartPlan (item, search_terms, item_context, price constraints), then hands it to code
→ "12 eggs" resolves to one carton of twelve via a deterministic quantity step, not free LLM arithmetic
→ A deterministic guardrail can veto a bad output and fall back before it ever reaches your cart
→ The lesson: when an agent is unreliable, the fix usually isn't a bigger model — it's taking responsibility away from the model and moving anything exact into code

The rule to steal: LLM handles meaning, code handles truth.

Andrej Karpathy's Four Principles (give these to Claude for your CLAUDE.md file) ⬇️

"## Coding Behavior

★ Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes (distilled from the verified Karpathy / agentic-engineering research; pairs with the `dev` CARL domain). Bias toward caution over speed; for trivial tasks, use judgment.

★ **Core discipline:** LLMs automate what you can *verify*. Define success criteria first, then loop until verified. You can outsource execution, never understanding.

1. ★ **Think before coding** — State assumptions explicitly; if uncertain, ask. If multiple interpretations exist, present them — don't pick silently. If a simpler approach exists, say so and push back. If something's unclear, stop and name it.
2. ★ **Simplicity first** — Minimum code that solves the problem, nothing speculative. No unrequested features, abstractions for single-use code, or error handling for impossible scenarios. If 200 lines could be 50, rewrite it.
3. ★ **Surgical changes** — Touch only what the request requires. Don't refactor or "improve" adjacent code; match existing style. Note unrelated dead code, don't delete it. Every changed line should trace to the request.
4. ★ **Goal-driven execution** — Convert vague asks into verifiable goals ("fix the bug" → "write a failing test that reproduces it, then make it pass"). For multi-step work, plan as `1. [step] → verify: [check]`.

★ Working if: fewer unnecessary diffs, fewer rewrites from overcomplication, and clarifying questions land *before* implementation. Reframed for delivery: spec = the brief, verifier = acceptance criteria, environment = the repeatable stack."

————————————

The black-footed cat is the smallest wild cat in Africa, weighing barely 1 to 3 kilograms, small enough to hold in one hand. It is also, by hunting success rate, the deadliest cat on the planet.
According to research by Panthera's Luke Hunter and field studies using radio collars, the black-footed cat has a predation success rate of around 60 percent, roughly three times higher than a lion's, which succeeds in only 20 to 25 percent of its hunting attempts. In a single night, it kills between 10 and 14 rodents, birds, or small reptiles, averaging a successful kill about every 50 minutes. Smithsonian Magazine reported that in one night, this cat kills more prey than a leopard does in six months.
This is not a demonstration of skill for its own sake. The black-footed cat has an extremely fast metabolism, forcing it to hunt almost continuously through the night just to sustain itself. It consumes close to one-fifth of its own body weight in a single night. Scaled to human terms, a 70 kilogram person would need to eat roughly 14 kilograms of food in one sitting to match that.
The cat hunts using three distinct techniques: fast pursuit through grass, slow stalking, and motionless sit-and-wait ambush near burrow entrances, sometimes holding still for up to two hours before striking. Despite its size, it can leap up to 1.4 metres to catch birds mid-flight and travel between 5 and 16 kilometres a night in search of prey.
Its appearance has nothing to do with its behaviour. Evolution built a compact, efficient predator, and camouflaged it as something harmless.
Source: Guinness World Records, Most Successful Feline Predator. LiveScience, Adorable Remorseless Killing Machine Is World's Deadliest Cat (2018). Smithsonian Magazine, This Petite Cat Is the World's Deadliest (2018).

Here's how to make Claude several times smarter in two minutes.

Stanford proved it: AI agrees with you 49 percent more often than a real human would. You ask for advice and get your own opinion handed back.

Andrej Karpathy, a co-founder of OpenAI, built the fix. It's called LLM Council.

You ask Claude a hard question, and instead of one answer it assembles five advisors. One attacks the idea, another hunts weak spots, a third looks from outside. They review each other anonymously, and a chairman gives the final verdict.

Cody Schneider is back on the podcast, and I ask him to lay out what a real marketing agent looks like once you get past the hype. He draws a hard line: an agent owns unified business data, runs on a cadence, and improves from the results it reads back. We use one concrete business as the sandbox — an AI-first product built on top of WordPress — and Cody walks the entire stack behind a Facebook ads agent that researches pain points, generates static and video creative, publishes through the Facebook Marketing API, kills the losers, and promotes the winners. You leave with a business idea, the exact infrastructure list, and the tools we use to run it today.

Key Points

* WordPress powers 43% of all indexed websites, which leaves a wide open lane for AI-first products built on that stack.

* A marketing agent earns the name when it owns live data, runs on a cadence, and learns from its own results.

* The infrastructure comes down to three pieces: a pipeline (Airbyte), a warehouse (ClickHouse), and cloud hosting (Heroku, Railway, or similar).

* Facebook's Andromeda algorithm reads your creative and your landing page, so the ad copy now carries the targeting.

* Fresh inputs — competitor ad libraries, YouTube transcripts, podcast transcripts — keep agent creative varied over time.

* Paid ads let you test a thousand angles and read the market's verdict inside 48 hours.

Numbered Section Summaries
1. What Counts as a Marketing Agent Cody sets the bar at three things: unified data across the whole pipeline, autonomous decisions on a cadence, and a thinking loop that reads results back. In practice that means a data pipeline, a data warehouse, and code hosted in the cloud — a definition that separates a working agent from a linear automation workflow.

2. AI for WordPress as the Sandbox The pitch is simple: a vibe-coding layer for WordPress that bundles the plugins people normally stitch together — forms, CRM, security — into one package sold on tokens, with a $29-per-month base tier. Cody sees a $10 million a year company inside roughly 24 months for a team that executes and positions it well.

3. Rebuilding Proven Plugins as AI-First Products I share my agency days migrating time.com and techcrunch.com onto WordPress, and the absurd money moving through the plugin ecosystem. That leads to a repeatable play: find plugins with validated demand, then ship the AI-first version — an agent that writes the meta and internal links in place of Yoast's red and green dots, a conversational form that qualifies leads, a WooCommerce storekeeper writing product descriptions and abandoned cart flows.

4. Creative Research That Seeds the Ads Cody runs Perplexity against Reddit to pull the real pain points and desired outcomes of WordPress site owners, then ranks them by how often people reference them. The top three — the plugin layer, performance and speed, and security and maintenance — become the ad angles, and he reads out the exact script shape that comes from them.

5. Generating Creative at Volume Statics come from Kai AI with Google Nano Banana, seeded by an example ad from a competitor or a tangential industry, with a vision model reviewing every output against brand style guides for fonts, colors, and readable text. Video runs on HeyGen for avatar UGC today, with Seedance coming up fast — clips cap out around nine seconds, so longer spots need frame stitching.

6. The Data Stack Behind the Agent Airbyte pipes Facebook ads, Google Analytics, CRM, and Stripe data into a ClickHouse warehouse so the agent sees the full path from ad to revenue. Cody keeps Facebook Marketing API usage to writes only — publish, pause, promote — because the account bans people blame on agents trace back to TOS violations from pulling hundreds of millions of rows.
